title: Three selectors, one question
spec: U05 · jit vs graph vs okf
intro: Selection is a family, not a technique. The same question, answered three different ways, all correct — and the receipts show three different shapes.
foot: Do it for real: pin Q9 and walk the toggle across jit → graph → okf

steps.title: The control: send everything
narrative: Start where U02 left off. Naive mode answers Q9 correctly for 1,700 tokens, 1,612 of them a dump of the entire seeded domain.
Three selectors are about to answer the same question correctly for under 300. They do it in three genuinely different ways, and knowing which one to reach for is the skill.

steps.title: Just-in-time — identifiers now, records on demand
narrative: JIT sends the model a thin index: which members exist, which requests belong to whom, and a tool that fetches a full record when asked. The bulky records stay out of the prompt until something needs them.

Watch the receipt's shape, not just its total. Retrieved collapses from 1,612 to 78, and a new layer appears: 54 tokens of tool results. That trade — retrieved down, tool up — is the signature of just-in-time.
steps.youDo: Set the mode toggle to jit and ask Q9 again.
steps.claudeSays: The model reads the index, sees M-2001 owns PA-1001 and PA-1004, and calls the fetch tool twice. It never sees a record it did not ask for.

terminal.text:
Member M-2001 has 2 authorization requests: PA-1001 APPROVED
(score 100); PA-1004 MANUAL_REVIEW (score 65).

after.title: AFTER — jit: retrieved down, tool up

steps.title: Graph — the subgraph instead of the dump
narrative: The graph selector walks relationships. It knows M-2001 is connected to two authorization nodes, pulls that neighbourhood, and sends only it. No index round-trip and no tool call — the selection happens before the model is ever invoked.
It costs 286 tokens, a little more than JIT. It earns that on relational questions where the answer depends on how records connect rather than what they contain.
steps.youDo: Switch to graph. Compare the tool layer with the JIT receipt you just read.

before.title: GRAPH — deterministic selection, no round trip

steps.title: OKF — one canonical file, zero search
narrative: The canonical selector does no searching at all. Somebody already wrote the concept file for member authorization history, and it is the right size by construction. The assembler loads it and stops.

190 tokens — the cheapest of the three, and the only one with no moving parts at query time. The cost moved from runtime to authoring time, which is a trade you make deliberately, not a saving you get for free.
steps.youDo: Switch to okf, then open the concept file the mode loaded and read it. That file is the whole trick.

steps.title: Three shapes, one verdict
narrative: All three are correct. All three are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than sending everything. They are not interchangeable: JIT pays a round trip and wins when you cannot predict what is needed; graph wins on relational questions; OKF wins when someone has already done the curation.
The lesson to carry into U06 is that selection is a family. "Use retrieval" is not a strategy. Choosing which selector fits the question class is.
